reason: This is the only available action and should start the muscle-cell lineage.
expectation: I expect the signals to produce muscle precursors from a subset of the stem-cell descendants.

effect: The signals produced myoblasts with muscle-related genes active, setting up their fusion.
reaction: The contrast with collagen-exporting fibroblasts makes the different cell roles clear.
reason: Fusion is the only offered combination and should form a multinucleated muscle cell.
expectation: I expect the myoblasts to join into a long cell containing multiple nuclei.

effect: The fused myoblasts have matured into a multinucleated fibre with actin–myosin units; their grip sites are still covered.
reaction: The one-cell outline makes the outcome of fusion clear.
reason: The calcium signal is the only offered combination and should initiate pulling.
expectation: I expect calcium to expose actin's grip sites so myosin can pull the filaments, though the precise steps may be shown next.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites, allowing ATP-dependent myosin cycles to slide the filaments; the fibre now needs to reset.
reaction: The distinction between sliding and filaments shortening is clear and useful.
reason: This is the only offered combination and should prepare the fibre to pull again.
expectation: I expect the pumps to use ATP to return calcium to storage, allowing the fibre to relax.

effect: Calcium pumping stopped pulling and reset the fibre; the next goal is to build and attach both muscles.
reaction: It is useful to see that relaxation requires ATP and an outside pull to lengthen the fibre.
reason: This is the only offered combination and should begin adding connective support around the muscle fibres.
expectation: I expect the extracellular matrix to help organize or support the fibres, though its precise role in building the muscles is not yet clear.

effect: The matrix now surrounds fibres and bundles as connective layers, creating fascicles for both muscles.
reaction: The distinction between a fibre's membrane and its surrounding connective tissue is helpful; the term fascicle is defined by the bundle label.
reason: I'll build the biceps first; both muscles are needed, and either appears a reasonable starting point.
expectation: I expect the fascicles to fill the biceps sheaths and connect to its tendons.

alternatives.reason: The triceps is also needed, but I have no clear reason to build it first.

effect: The biceps fascicles now fill two heads, with connective tissue carrying their force into the tendons.
reaction: The force-path inset makes the tendon connection useful rather than just a placement.
reason: I'll build the triceps next so both muscles are ready to attach.
expectation: I expect fascicles to fill the three triceps heads and connect to their tendons.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the biceps now would also advance the goal, but I prefer to assemble both muscles first.

effect: Both muscles are assembled; the triceps has three heads converging at the ulna, with different proximal origins.
reaction: The outline clarifies that one triceps head crosses the shoulder as well as the elbow.
reason: I'll attach the biceps first; both attachments are needed and either is a reasonable start.
expectation: I expect the biceps tendons to attach across the elbow, linking the shoulder and radius to the skeleton.

alternatives.reason: Attaching the triceps first would also advance the goal, but the order seems unimportant.

effect: The biceps is attached across the front of the elbow and can flex it; the extensor slot remains empty.
reaction: The paired poses clarify how the biceps pull bends the elbow.
reason: The triceps is the only offered combination and should fill the extensor slot.
expectation: I expect the triceps tendons to attach across the elbow so its pull can extend the arm.

effect: The triceps fills the extensor slot, completing the arm and showing how its attachment produces the opposite elbow movement from the biceps.
reaction: The paired movements make the relationship between muscle position and action clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: The calcium-triggered sliding cycle was most worthwhile: the planned sequence connects calcium and ATP to pulling while distinguishing filament sliding from filament shortening.

leastWorthwhile.text: Assembling the two muscles was somewhat repetitive, although the different head and tendon arrangements added useful detail.

surprise.text: Relaxation requires ATP-powered calcium pumping, and the fibre lengthens under an outside pull rather than actively pushing itself longer.

arbitrary.text: Choosing biceps before triceps felt arbitrary: both were needed, and the menu gave no clear reason to prefer either order.

continue.text: I would continue: the progression from cellular machinery to opposing movements made the constructions meaningful, despite several forced choices.
